1212.title: Following another school
1212.hook: many scholars allow following another school's view in some cases
1212.howItsDone: Muslims who follow a school usually keep to its rulings, and when a hard case arises some ask a scholar whether another school's view may be followed; some scholars allow it for genuine need and warn against picking the easiest view each time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, witr in many ways, and your line: odd, in any way.

A question lands on a scholar's desk. A woman's husband left home and never came back. No letter. No word. No grave. Her family follows the Hanafi school, and in its classical books the answer is hard: she waits a very long time before a judge may declare her free to marry again. The Maliki books give a judge room to act after a far shorter wait. So the scholar has two answers in front of him, one from his own school and one from a neighbor's. He can keep the door shut, or open it. Today: following another school.
screen: `A HUSBAND WHO NEVER CAME BACK.` → `TWO SCHOOLS, TWO ANSWERS.` → `KEEP THE DOOR SHUT, OR OPEN IT?`

segments.voice: A Muslim who isn't a jurist usually follows a school. Earlier in this block that had a name, taqlid: trusting a madhhab's method instead of rebuilding the law alone. So can a person step outside it? The jurists don't give one answer. Some held that once you take a school, you keep to it. Others allow following another school's view in some cases. Back to the missing husband. Hanafi scholars in South Asia, facing wives left in exactly that limbo, wrote a work that drew on the Maliki position, so a judge could end the marriage and the woman could go on with her life. The door was opened for a need, and through a judge, not on a whim. Some of those who allow it point to a line about fasting in surah two, in Pickthall's words: "Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you." Then the warning on the other side of the door. The jurists have a phrase for picking whichever school's view is lightest, in matter after matter, just because it's lightest: tatabbu' ar-rukhas, chasing the concessions. And there's a related debate over talfiq, stitching: washing for prayer by one school's rule and praying by another's, so that the whole act might count in no single school. Some scholars forbid it; some allow it within limits. In practice, a person with a real difficulty asks someone who knows both schools, and the answer comes with a reason. Not a hole knocked in the wall. A door, with a frame.
screen: `TAQLID: KEEPING TO ONE SCHOOL.` · `A DOOR OPENED FOR A NEED.` · `NOT CHASING THE LIGHTEST VIEW.` · `ASK, AND HEAR THE REASON.` · then, large: `ALLAH DESIRETH FOR YOU EASE.`

segments.voice: Let your breathing slow. Bring to mind a time someone made room for you, a deadline moved, a rule bent, because your situation really was hard, and a time you asked for the easy way only because it was easy. Hold the two side by side, without judging either; if you pray, you can ask for understanding in your own words.
Following another school. Some scholars allow taking another school's view in some cases, for a real need, with a reason, and they warn against chasing whatever is lightest. Today's word.
Your line: doors between schools. A real need, a real reason, and someone who knows. See you tomorrow.

1213.title: Praying behind another
1213.hook: Muslims of different schools pray behind one another
1213.howItsDone: In mosques with people from different schools, worshippers stand in one straight row behind one imam, each keeping their own school's details, such as where the hands are placed, while following the imam's movements.

segments.voice: Yesterday, following another school: a door opened for a need, with a reason. Your line: doors between schools.

A traveler steps off a bus in a city she has never seen, bag still on her shoulder, and follows the sound of the call to the nearest mosque. The prayer has already started. She doesn't know the imam's name, which school his teachers followed, or how he was taught to wash before he stood up there. She slips into the end of the last row, closes the gap beside a stranger, and raises her hands with everyone else. Should she have asked first? Does her prayer depend on details she can't see? Today: praying behind another.
screen: `A STRANGE CITY, A STRANGE MOSQUE.` → `AN IMAM SHE DOESN'T KNOW.` → `SHE JOINS THE ROW.`

segments.voice: The jurists asked it plainly. If the imam follows one school and I follow another, does my prayer behind him count? They argued over whose rules decide it, the imam's school or the follower's. Some judged that if the imam's prayer is sound by his own school, the people behind him may follow him. Others added conditions. But the row kept forming. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said of those who lead the prayer, in meaning, they lead you, and if they get it right, it's for you and for them, and if they get it wrong, it's for you and against them. The follower's prayer isn't hostage to every detail of the imam's. Then a story told in later books about Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal. In his view, bleeding called for a fresh wudu. Someone asked whether he would pray behind an imam who had bled and not washed again, following a school that didn't require it. The answer, as the story goes: how could I not pray behind Malik, or Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib? Great scholars, whose view on bleeding wasn't his. Last, the row itself. In Bukhari, the Prophet tells the people to straighten their rows, and calls that part of establishing the prayer. Anas, a companion, describes them standing shoulder to shoulder, foot to foot. The row is built from bodies, not opinions: a Hanafi shoulder against a Shafi'i shoulder, the gap closed. In Mecca, pilgrims from different schools pray behind the imams of the Sacred Mosque. The hands differ. The row doesn't.
screen: `WHOSE RULES DECIDE IT?` · `IF HE ERRS, IT IS AGAINST HIM.` · `HOW COULD I NOT PRAY BEHIND MALIK?` · `SHOULDER TO SHOULDER, FOOT TO FOOT.`

segments.voice: Sit or stand tall and feel your shoulders. Imagine a shoulder on either side touching yours, a stranger, a neighbor, someone whose way you don't share, and breathe with them. Don't fix their hands, and don't fix yours.
Praying behind another. Muslims of different schools stand in one row behind one imam, and the jurists worked out how each person's prayer still counts. Today's word.
Your line: one row. Different hands, and still no gap. Rest well.

1214.title: Why they differ
1214.hook: different reports, readings, and methods, all seeking the same thing
1214.howItsDone: Muslim students of law learn not only their school's rulings but the reasons schools differ, such as a word with two meanings, a report that reached one scholar and not another, or a different way of weighing evidence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, praying behind another: different schools, one row. Your line: one row.

One word in the Qur'an, and the schools read it two ways. Surah two, verse two hundred twenty-eight, in Pickthall's translation: "Women who are divorced shall wait, keeping themselves apart, three (monthly) courses." The Arabic word behind those courses is quru'. It can mean the monthly periods themselves, or the clean days between them. The Hanafi and Hanbali schools count the periods. The Maliki and Shafi'i schools count the clean intervals. Nobody skipped the verse. They all read it carefully and sincerely, and the word itself held two doors open. Today: why they differ.
screen: `THREE (MONTHLY) COURSES.` → `QURU': PERIODS, OR THE DAYS BETWEEN?` → `ONE VERSE, TWO HONEST READINGS.`

segments.voice: That's the first reason: readings. Arabic words can carry more than one meaning, and the schools sometimes chose differently. The second: reports. Not every hadith reached every scholar. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps a story about Umar, the caliph. Abu Musa came to his door, asked permission three times, heard no answer, and left. Umar called him back and asked why. Abu Musa said the Prophet ﷺ had taught it: ask three times, and if there's no answer, go. Umar had never heard it, and he wanted a witness. Abu Sa'id stood up and confirmed it. And Umar said, in meaning, that trading in the markets had kept him busy. If the caliph could miss a report, so could a scholar in another city. The third: methods. Once the reports are in hand, how do you weigh them? Imam Malik gave weight to the living practice of the people of Medina. Other schools leaned more on analogy, or on a lone report with a strong chain. Each method is a way of being careful. Ibn Taymiyya later wrote a short book, Raf' al-Malam, the removal of blame from the great imams, to explain why a sound scholar might leave a hadith aside: it hadn't reached him, he doubted its chain, or he read it another way. The fourth: what they share. In Bukhari, the Prophet says that when a judge strives and gets it right, he has two rewards, and when he strives and gets it wrong, he has one. The striving itself is rewarded. Hands, amin, touch, the moon, witr, other schools, the row: underneath every one, the same search.
screen: `ONE WORD, TWO MEANINGS.` · `A REPORT THAT DIDN'T REACH HIM.` · `DIFFERENT WAYS OF WEIGHING.` · `TWO REWARDS, OR ONE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one honest person who disagrees with you about something that matters, someone real, not the loudest voice online, and picture them at their kitchen table, working it out. Ask what they might have read, or heard, or weighed that you haven't; you don't have to change your mind, just let them be someone who is seeking too. If you pray, remember them kindly.
Why they differ. Different readings of a word, different reports that reached them, different methods of weighing, all seeking the same thing. Today's word.
Your line: seeking the same. Different roads, different readings, and one search under them all. Until tomorrow.

1215.title: Who gives a fatwa
1215.hook: a mufti gives a non-binding answer to a question
1215.howItsDone: Muslims with a question about prayer, fasting, money or family may ask a local imam or a trained mufti, in person, by phone or online; the answer, a fatwa, advises the person who asked and is not a court ruling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why they differ: readings, reports and methods. Your line: seeking the same.

A message sits in a mosque's inbox, typed late at night. Years ago I was sick and missed days of Ramadan. I never made them up. What do I owe now? No name, maybe. No drama. Just a person with a question they can't answer alone. Somewhere, someone trained in the law will read it, maybe ask a follow-up, and write back. That written answer has a name, a word that has picked up a heavy sound in the headlines. Here it means something quieter. A new stretch of the path starts today: law in life. Today's word: fatwa.
screen: `A QUESTION IN THE INBOX.` → `SOMEONE WHO KNOWS WRITES BACK.` → `LAW IN LIFE BEGINS.`

segments.voice: A fatwa is an answer to a question about the law. The one who answers is a mufti. In the Qur'an, people bring questions to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and the asking itself is there in the text. Surah four, near its end, in Pickthall: "They ask thee for a pronouncement. Say: Allah hath pronounced for you concerning distant kindred." Someone asks; an answer comes. Why ask at all? Surah sixteen says, in Pickthall: "Ask the followers of the Remembrance if ye know not." Commentators read it first about the prophets of earlier times, and jurists also drew from it a wider rule: when you don't know, ask someone who does. Now, what a fatwa is not. It is not a court verdict. A mufti answers the person who asked, about the situation they described. It advises. It doesn't sentence, and it doesn't bind the way a judge's ruling does. The answer can change if the facts change. And a mufti is allowed, even expected, to say he doesn't know; the biographies remember Imam Malik answering questions with: I don't know. Last, the asker still carries something. A man named Wabisa came to the Prophet wanting to ask about righteousness and sin. In a report in Musnad Ahmad, the Prophet tells him to consult his own heart: righteousness is what the soul is at ease with, and sin is what wavers inside, even if people give you fatwas, and give you fatwas again. Ask one who knows. Then listen inside, too.
screen: `FATWA: AN ANSWER TO A QUESTION.` · `ASK, IF YE KNOW NOT.` · `ADVICE, NOT A VERDICT.` · `CONSULT YOUR HEART, TOO.`

segments.voice: Breathe out slowly and find one thing about your practice, your family or your money that you've been guessing about. Say it to yourself plainly, in one sentence, the way you'd type it into a message, and notice whether it feels heavy or just unfinished. Then let it rest; if you pray, you can ask for a clear answer in your own words.
Fatwa. An answer to a question about the law, given by a mufti to the one who asked: advice, not a verdict. Today's word.
Your line: ask one who knows. A fatwa advises, and the heart still listens. I'll be here tomorrow.

1216.title: The judge
1216.hook: a judge rules in disputes, bound by evidence
1216.howItsDone: In Islamic law a qadi, a judge, hears disputes and rules on the evidence; in some countries qadis or family courts still hear cases about marriage and inheritance, and Muslims elsewhere sometimes bring such matters to religious arbitration.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fatwa: a mufti's answer, advice and not a verdict. Your line: ask one who knows.

I am only a human being. That's not a defendant talking. In a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, it's the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, speaking as a judge. People bring their quarrels to him, he says, and one of them may argue his case better than the other, so he rules by what he hears. Then a warning to whoever wins: if I hand you something that's really your brother's, I'm handing you a piece of fire. A judge who admits he can be fooled, and puts the weight back on the people in front of him. Today's word: qadi.
screen: `I AM ONLY A HUMAN BEING.` → `ONE ARGUES BETTER THAN THE OTHER.` → `A PIECE OF FIRE.`

segments.voice: A qadi is a judge, the one who decides between people. Yesterday's mufti gives an answer, and the asker can weigh it. A qadi gives a ruling, and the parties in the case are bound by it. The tradition fenced that heavier job with rules. First, the command. Surah four, in Pickthall's translation: "if ye judge between mankind, that ye judge justly." Second, the hadith from the hook. The Prophet judges by what he hears. A ruling decides the case in front of the court; it doesn't turn a lie into the truth. The one who wins by clever talk still answers for what he took. Third, who has to prove what. A saying gathered by an-Nawawi in his Forty Hadith, from al-Bayhaqi: if people were given whatever they claimed, some would claim the property and even the lives of others. So the proof is on the one who makes the claim, and the oath is on the one who denies it. The judge starts from evidence, not a hunch, and when there's none, from an oath. Fourth, the judge's own state. In Bukhari, a companion passes on the Prophet's words that a judge should not decide between two people while he is angry. Not won over by the better speaker. Bound by what can be shown. Some scholars of the early generations are remembered for refusing the job of qadi altogether, because they feared its weight. The tradition treats the seat as a trust, and an uncomfortable one.
screen: `QADI: THE ONE WHO DECIDES.` · `I JUDGE BY WHAT I HEAR.` · `PROOF ON THE ONE WHO CLAIMS.` · `NEVER WHILE ANGRY.` · then, large: `THAT YE JUDGE JUSTLY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a disagreement you're part of right now and sit in the judge's seat: what do you actually know, what are you assuming, and what would the other person say if they spoke as well as you do? If you're angry, just notice it, and let one breath out longer than the rest; if you pray, you can ask in your own words to be fair.
Qadi. A judge who rules in disputes, bound by evidence: proof from the one who claims, an oath from the one who denies. Today's word.
Your line: judge by evidence. What can be shown, not what sounds best. See you tomorrow.

1217.title: Marriage as contract
1217.hook: consent of both, a gift to the bride, witnesses, a public celebration
1217.howItsDone: A Muslim marriage is concluded by an offer and acceptance before witnesses, sometimes led by an imam at a mosque or at home, with the bride's consent, an agreed gift to the bride, and a celebration afterward.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the qadi, a judge bound by evidence. Your line: judge by evidence.

A living room, packed. Aunts on the sofa, kids on the stairs, someone's phone held up to film. On the coffee table, a sheet of paper. A man asks a question, and a young man answers it out loud: I accept. Somewhere in the room, or just before, the bride has said her yes too. Two people lean in to sign as witnesses. There's a line on the paper for a gift to the bride. Then someone says mubarak, and the room breaks into noise. No vows invented on the spot. A question, an answer, a signature, a cheer. Today's word: nikah.

segments.voice: Nikah is the Arabic word for marriage, and in Islamic law a nikah is a contract. Its heart is an offer and an acceptance, spoken out loud, in one sitting. One side offers; the other says I accept. That's the knot. Next, the consent of both. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says a woman is not to be married until her permission is sought. And Bukhari keeps the story of Khansa bint Khidam, whose father married her to a man she didn't want. She went to the Prophet, and he annulled the marriage. Her yes was not decoration. Then the other parts. A gift to the bride, the mahr, which is tomorrow. Witnesses, so the marriage isn't a secret. A public celebration, so the whole neighborhood knows. Here the schools differ on details. The Hanafi school allows a grown woman to conclude her own marriage contract; the Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools require a guardian, a wali, to conclude it for her, with her consent. They also differ on how the witnessing and the announcing have to be done. Last, why a contract isn't cold. The Qur'an calls the marriage bond a firm, weighty covenant. And in surah thirty it describes marriage this way, in Pickthall's translation: "He created for you helpmeets from yourselves that ye might find rest in them, and He ordained between you love and mercy." The paper sets out rights, and the verse sets out what the paper is for: rest, love, mercy. A contract, yes. A contract of mercy.

segments.voice: With each breath, set one part down on the coffee table from the hook: her yes and his, the offer and the acceptance, the gift, the witnesses, the celebration. Then hold a marriage you know, or one you hope for, with two words from the verse: love and mercy. If you pray, you can remember that couple in your own words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the nikah: offer, acceptance and the consent of both. Your line: a contract of mercy.

A man stands up in the mosque in Medina. A woman has come to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and this man asks to marry her. The Prophet asks him: what do you have to give her? Nothing, he says, only this cloth I'm wearing. If you give her that, the Prophet says, you'll be sitting there with nothing on. Go and look for something, even an iron ring. The man goes. He comes back. Not even an iron ring. The story, in Sahih al-Bukhari, isn't over. But notice what's being searched for, so hard: something for her. Today's word: mahr.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU HAVE TO GIVE HER?` → `ONLY THIS CLOTH.` → `EVEN AN IRON RING.`

segments.voice: Mahr is the bride's gift, given by the groom, and it's part of yesterday's nikah. Surah four, verse four, names it, in Pickthall's translation: "And give unto the women (whom ye marry) free gift of their marriage portions." A free gift. Not a price paid for a person, not a fee to her family. Whose is it? In Islamic law the mahr belongs to the bride. Not to her father, not to her brothers, not to a shared account. Hers. The same verse says that if she chooses, of her own accord, to give some of it back, that's her call. And a little further on, the Qur'an tells husbands not to take back what they gave, even if it was a great amount. Now the story from the hook. The man came back without even a ring. So the Prophet asked: what do you know of the Qur'an? The man named some surahs he knew by heart, and the Prophet married them for what he knew of the Qur'an. Some versions say he was to teach them to her. The gift doesn't have to be gold. It does have to be hers. Today, some couples agree a mahr paid at the wedding, some write part of it into the contract to be paid later, and the schools differ on details like whether there's a minimum. This week ran from schools to law in life: other schools, one row, why they differ, the fatwa, the judge, the nikah, and now the gift. By its end, the questions had turned into who owes what to whom.
